speechtext: The House resumed from Tuesday, September 1, consideration of the motion of Mr. Wise that Bill C-2, an Act to dissolve Canagrex and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof, be read the third time and passed.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to complete my remarks regarding the death of Canagrex.
The only thing that we can hope for is that the Mulroney Government will call an election soon in order that we can get on with re-establishing some form of Canagrex to assist the Canadian family farm, and the small exporters of the country. Based on the results of recent times, I suspect that that is in the offing. I hope that an election is called as soon as possible in order that we can complete this discussion of Canagrex and move to something more positive.
It is important that we recognize what Canagrex did in the very short time that it was in existence. I remember in the winter of 1984, after the Government had shifted, some questions were put to the Hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise). One question was, what were the total expenditures on Canagrex? Another question was, what was the result of those expenditures? Did we receive our money's worth? Did the taxpayers of Canada receive what they deserved in terms of their investment in Canagrex?
The Minister of Agriculture advised that the total expenditures to establish Canagrex had amounted to $2.6 million. He then went on to add how delighted he was with the accomplishments of this federal agency. He advised that when the corporation began operations in the spring of 1984, policy focused on facilitating sales by bringing a willing buyer and a seller into a negotiating position rather than on purchasing products or selling for the corporation's account.
I wish to remind Members that Canagrex was not involved in buying and selling agricultural products. That was clearly to be left to the private sector, to the international exporting companies as well as the commodity groups themselves, with one exception. The Hon. Member from Fraser Valley, who is obviously interested in agricultural exports, will remember that many countries arranged food or agricultural exports and imports on a government to government basis, and simply did not work with specific companies or individual firms. For that reason Canagrex was playing a rather unique role, because it could move a Government of Canada arrangement with the government of country x. Again, that would facilitate the export of our excellent agricultural products.
The Hon. Minister went on to say that Canagrex was involved in negotiations leading to the facilitation of sales worth $16 million, and in addition there were transactions in progress worth a potential $100 million to be finalized on March 31, 1985.
Considering the red tape and the hurdles that were thrown up in front of Canagrex in its first few weeks and months of operation, the fact that it accomplished so much in so little time is really quite astounding, quite amazing. The response from the family farms across Canada, and the small exporters was quite phenomenal.
I remember touring my constituency of Kamloops- Shuswap where we raise a lot of food, beef, poultry, poultry by-products, dairy products, berry products, some grains, many vegetables, soft fruits-I could go on in terms of incredibly productive farms; almost inevitably they are family operations, and they were struggling and continue to struggle against the subsidized agricultural exporters of Europe, and particularly the United States. I remember we were up against the American GSM-102 and GSM-105 programs which literally made it impossible for our family farms to compete head to head with the operations in the United States, and particularly in Europe, in countries such as the United Kingdom, France, and Germany. We needed some help then, and we still do.

Unless something quite dramatic is done by the Government in a very short period of time, I am afraid that our commitment to the family farm operation in this country will go the way of the dinosaur. We cannot compete under present conditions. We need to recognize the reality of the international commodity market-place. Therefore, I think that Canagrex was a step in the right direction.

September 11, 1987
Canagrex
My hon. friends opposite disagree. That is fair enough; that is why we are here. If we agreed on everything it simply would not be the Parliament of Canada. I say that the track record of Canagrex was second to none.
In digging through my files in preparation for this speech- and perhaps I should have dug a little deeper-I came across the first thing that happened with Canagrex, and it happened day after day. I have a stack of press releases in my office showing the successes of Canagrex. On August 29, 1984, the Minister of Agriculture announced a $50 million line of credit to export the sale of food and agricultural products from Canada. They had facilitated a line of credit with a Canadian bank and a foreign bank which the Minister thought would result in $25 million of Canadian agri-food products flowing out of Canada within a few weeks, including such products as soya bean meal, corn, seed potatoes, beans, and turkeys. This is only one press release, but it is important to remember that these exports would not have taken place had Canagrex not been in the international market-place opening up market opportunities for our farmers.
It did not operate in competition with existing systems. We have private exporters and private firms opening up new markets. We have Agriculture Canada, CIDA, and trade offices trying to find more markets. Canagrex was designed to fill in the cracks, because there were many countries in which we were not-and we still are not-attempting to open up new markets for Canadian food products. We have a long way to
go-
I cannot imagine why anyone would have opposed such a paltry sum of $12.4 million being set aside for Canagrex over a three-year period to facilitate this federal agency in the opening of new markets. I have not met a single person in the food producing sector who says that Canada should not have a federal agency like every other food producing country in the western world to facilitate the establishment of new markets.
Where is the evidence that this is wrong? One of the last farm groups to appear before the committee when we looked at the demise of Canagrex was the National Farmers Union, represented by Mr. Wayne Easter. He indicated how this was a slap in the face to Canadian farmers.
In some sectors the industry is virtually in a crisis or emergency situation. In many respects it requires rescue money because of the problems in which it finds itself. However, here was a relatively inexpensive initiative to provide assistance to the family farm operation in east, west and central Canada. However, the Conservative Government mysteriously wants to abandon this initiative. It was given a paltry sum of $12.4 million over a three-year period, and now we are driving the last spike into the coffin of Canagrex.
In conclusion, every shred of evidence when it comes to Canagrex indicates that it is a good idea, concept, and initiative. It is a good agency. It is something the Government of Canada could be and should be doing for our farmers, not
abandoning the agency and by definition abandoning Canadian food producers who rank highest in the world in terms of their ability to produce food in efficient and effective ways.
I look forward to the demise of the Progressive Conservative Government so that whatever replaces it-and hopefully it will be a New Democratic Party Government-will be able to reinstitute a new version of Canagrex, a version which will enable it to fulfil its mandate to assist the family farm operation in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) spent some time talking about the role which Canagrex was attempting to play before the Government brought it to an untimely end.
I should like to note that the decision to oppose Canagrex came slowly to the Conservatives. Upon the introduction of the Bill by the then Minister of Agriculture, Eugene Whelan, the then House Leader of the Conservative Party, Erik Nielsen, in a very unusual step, rose in the House and welcomed the initiative on behalf of the Government and indicated that Canagrex was something for which the Hon. Member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) had been preparing when he was Minister of Agriculture in the short term 1979 Conservative Government. He indicated that his Party welcomed with open arms the initiative.
The first several speakers from the Tory benches in that period of time also spoke in favour of Canagrex, until the Hon. Member for Etobicoke Centre, the current Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), made a speech damning the whole concept. Conservative attitudes gradually changed until they became very firmly entrenched against the institution of Canagrex.
One reason for indicating that it was not necessary in their opinion was that we have commercial counsellors in some of our embassies overseas who can direct interest in agricultural business back to Canada. These counsellors have been at work since the demise of Canagrex, and there has virtually been no indication that their work has resulted in more exports. On occasion they contact the Canadian Wheat Board, which is one of the better marketing agencies in the world. They are able to complete sales, but these commercial counsellors have no one to turn to for other commodities. That was a role Canagrex could play.
One of the first things it did was to establish with the buyers and sellers in the industry the fact that Canagrex would play a facilitating role and that the buying, selling, and taking of commissions, an important concern of the Minister of Finance, would be left as is. Canagrex was simply to have the list of buyers and sellers and put the two together, and normal commercial channels would carry out the actual finalization of sales.
Canagrex no longer exists as a facilitator. Unfortunately for trading operations that spoke against Canagrex, they do not have the business. Nobody gains.

Could the Hon. Member tell me what advantage the country seems to be getting now that the Conservative Government has done away with Canagrex? How do honey producers complete sales overseas? How do potato producers or some of the small bean operators do so when they do not have a very large marketing organization of their own?

Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) has put his finger on the nub of the problem. The clientele of Canagrex tended to be small, independent producers, the fledgling enterprises in our producing sector that were trying to get established; in other words, where the growth and the future of agriculture lie. Canagrex was really interested in helping these groups, individuals, and organizations. Large agricultural organizations had their markets established and perhaps did not need the same kind of assistance.
I should like to refer to a press release when the Government first indicated that it planned to do away with Canagrex. It noted that Canagrex saw the need for a federal agency that would facilitate the export of Canadian foodstuffs. Farmers and small exporters defended it enthusiastically while larger established corporate agriculture opposed it, and here perhaps we have the real essence of the matter.
The large corporate agri-business said, "We don't want any more competition, we have the market sewn up, the financial cash flows, the organizations, the cartels and monopolies in place. We don't want competition. We don't want the small enterpriser, the small operator or the small exporter getting involved. We have been working on this for a long time and we have it set up."
But whose side ought we be on? Whose side should Parliament be supporting, large agri-corporate business or the small independent producer? We say we should be supporting the small independent producer whenever and wherever possible. We should be assisting that individual farmer, that small agency, the small co-op. That is who we should be supporting, not agri-business. Is the Government saying in this Bill that we support our corporate friends but we are prepared to abandon the small family farm?

Mr. Speaker, Canada is a producing country. Agriculture is very important for our economy. We are fighting the demise of the family farm. We want to see agriculture remain a very important part of Canada. That is why we are very disturbed with the sudden death of Canagrex, a death ordered by the Conservative Government in spite of the fact that in times past when the Conservatives were a little more practical they were in favour of Canagrex.
Why were the Conservatives in favour and why did they change their minds? They were in favour of Canagrex for the same reasons we were initially-there was a clear need for it.
Canagrex
Marketing boards did not cover all subjects. Independent producers needed assistance in selling their produce.
In 1982 we had $9.5 billion worth of exports in agriculture and a surplus of $3.1 billion, 60 per cent of which was in grains and oilseeds with a very serious trade deficit in the non-grain area of $2 billion. There was an opportunity to do something about that; to improve our exports in the other areas, those outside wheat where there are strong marketing facilities already through the Wheat Board. Canagrex was to fill this gap in our marketing strategy. To have a sane agricultural policy we must have production and marketing. It does not make sense to have one without the other. A comprehensive policy and very practical measures are needed to ensure that the whole system works, and Canagrex was designed to fill that gap.
Interestingly when the Bill was introduced at first reading, the Conservatives supported it. The Bill was brought in by the Liberals and at that time at first reading the Conservative House Leader rose to speak and pointed out that the Conservatives in the brief period they were in government had already worked on Canagrex and were in favour of it. The Conservatives were trying to do practical things at that time. Then suddenly, midstage, for ideological reasons, there was an about-face. The Conservatives opposed Canagrex. When the Conservatives returned to office in 1984, Canagrex had already been set up. It had not been in operation very long. Suddenly the Conservative Government wanted to chop it and indeed it did. The Government did not give Canagrex a chance to show how effective it could be. The decision was made within a matter of months and Canagrex was told to wind up its operation.
In the very brief time that Canagrex was in operation, however, it was beginning to have a positive impact which was helping farmers. Built into the legislation was the fact that buying and selling would be left to the private sector and Canagrex's objective was to facilitate sales and provide information. Canagrex gathered the information. It prepared a survey of Canadian commodities available for export. This important information was essential, especially since the number of commodities in surplus supply or which were available for export since 1984 was very limited. That source list of Canadian commodities is probably the most comprehensive and up to date available anywhere today.
Canagrex developed a market survey program. This meant in-depth research on specific market areas which were considered to be potentially promising for Canadian farm exports. The market research people travelled to countries accompanied by producers who could talk about their products on the spot. For example, Canagrex had a pork producer accompany its mission to Singapore and a potato producer travelled to Cuba for sales. Canagrex prepared comprehensive studies to identify market prospects for a number of important export commodities. A major study was prepared on pork, which was well-received by the Canadian industry. Other studies were prepared on the export potential for honey and

September 11, 1987
Canagrex
processed foods. Again, these studies were done in co-operation with the industry groups. The people in the know, doing the work and producing, had input into sales preparation.
Canagrex undertook a program to stimulate export sales abroad. It defrayed some of the costs involved in transporting high quality breeding swine to Italy on the understanding that out of any subsequent sales Canagrex would recover its expenses. There was a happy result from this one. The Canadian swine won several medals at a Milan exhibition and foreign buyers visited Canada to investigate further purchases. This very modest initiative resulted in buyers coming to Canada to make their own deals of Canadian stock purchases.
Another example was a buyers credit guarantee program. Under this program Canagrex agreed to share a certain amount of the risk involved in providing credit to a buyer to purchase Canadian agricultural commodities in addition to its normal purchases. Under this program, Canagrex sought to have the risks shared among the exporters, the banks or the insurance companies and the foreign buyer. A Canagrex guarantee was provided when it was deemed absolutely necessary. It was to be used sparingly but available as one thing that could be done to increase exports for our producers. A combination of aid and trade at lower effective interest rates was part of the strategy.
In certain instances Canagrex was faced with similar programs offered by the French, German and British Governments which made selling certain commodities on a cash basis virtually impossible. Our producers have to compete with producers in other countries. When other countries have programs supporting their producers, we fail our producers if we do not meet them in kind. Our producers, especially grain producers, face the enormous subsidy programs that other countries have for their producers. That is the world, and how very nice it would be to change it and change the rules, but while other countries are providing support, we have to ensure that our own producers do not lose out in the process.
Canadian agricultural exporters were desperate for some assistance to maintain and increase their market sales and Canagrex was there to help in situations when other countries were able to do very much more for their producers.
One of the things that is most disturbing about the Government is the very rapid way it has proceeded without consultation. It made a decision on ideological grounds. The agency had been set up, it was starting to work and to be effective. The Government did not give it a chance to complete a fiscal year and have a proper review of its successes to that date. The Government did not call for public hearings or ask the producers what they wanted done. Nor did it ask the Canagrex people themselves. The decision was made, the guillotine fell and that was tough luck.
But that is not an appropriate way to operate, Mr. Speaker. People were in place making a contribution and doing the job that Parliament gave them to do. It seems to me that it would have been very much more sensible if the Conservatives felt for
ideological reasons that they were against Canagrex to review the situation and look at the actual record before making the decision. Why not at least ensure that the right decision is being made? We in this Party do not like to see these kinds of abstract, ideological decisions made without reference to the actual facts, the real situation in the industry itself.
Certainly the farmers themselves and the National Farmers Union, for example, were very concerned that they were not consulted. Wayne Easter, the President of the National Farmers Union, criticized the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) for playing politics in his Budget speech and for moving so quickly to eliminate the newly created Crown agency. He said:
"The new government is obviously playing politics," explained Easter. "While the Tories were opposed to the creation of Canagrex on ideological grounds, there is no justification for closing down the agency while it is still in its infancy. Canagrex should be given some time to prove its worth both to farmers and to the Canadian public."
It seems to me that that is a perfectly reasonable approach. Even in the face of the Conservative ideological position, the Government could have held off for a few months and given Canagrex a chance. It could have given the producers themselves the opportunity to say whether or not it was helping their sales abroad.
The National Farmers Union President noted that the move to slash Canagrex illustrated the Government's misguided priorities in regard to the agriculture sector. Rather than taking action on very pressing issues like farm finance, low commodity prices and interest rates, the Government chose instead to talk about the problem. Other areas which would more properly be dealt with through greater discussion, such as Canagrex, were instead subjected to immediate and damaging action.
I think this is one of the things we are concerned about. Prompt action was taken for ideological reasons on something that was not a problem. We certainly have not had any reason to think that there was a problem with Canagrex because it was not in operation for long enough to see if it was a problem. Certainly the First reports indicated that Canagrex was acting efficiently and effectively. Yet all these other far more important problems were not dealt with. Problems like farmers losing their farms, suffering from low prices and not being able to pay off their bank loans are crucial problems, but they are being neglected so that the Conservatives can pursue a policy determined abstractly in a back room somewhere after reading the works of Margaret Thatcher or something to that effect.
The President of the National Farmers Union suggested that the Government should at least have waited until March 31, the end of the Government's fiscal year, in order to give the agency time to get established. Then the more appropriate course would have been to put Canagrex on the carpet by holding public hearings to assess the value of the agency. Bygiving Canagrex the opportunity to justify its existence and by
September 11, 1987

allowing farmers to make an informed choice on whether or not the agency is worth while, an educated decision could have been made.
I am sorry to see that the decision that has been made is not an educated one. It is an abstract, theoretical, ideological decision and that is not what Canadians want. Canadians want practicality, particularly for smaller, independent producers who do not have big business behind them, the ones who do not have access to stronger marketing agencies. Those are the people Parliament ought to have foremost in its mind when providing assistance to agriculture.
There seems to be no doubt among people who have followed Canagrex's very short career that even during the period it was in operation, it demonstrated that there was an important need for export assistance for agricultural producers. Most other sectors of Canada's exporting community have specific instruments which can provide assistance in selling their products abroad. Of course, in big business, the corporations themselves are strong. In other sectors, there is government assistance in marketing.
For example, the industrial sector has the Export Development Corporation which has a budget that allows it to provide enormous assistance by way of loans, insurance, marketing advice and contacts. All of these kinds of things are provided in other sectors. It seems to be extremely unfair that this very modest agency in the agricultural sector with its very small budget which had begun to meet a need should be chopped.
Producers need assistance in selling their very fine products. The problem is not with production, it is with exports. The problem is in getting those crops out into the markets and starting to reverse the very substantial trade deficit in nongrain agricultural products. This of course can be absolutely vital to the economy.
We already have efficient producers in the renewable resources. We depend so much for our exports on resources that are not renewable while agriculture is renewable. This is the kind of economic measure we would like to see developed. We want to see more emphasis put on renewable resources in a concerted way through production, sales and marketing to ensure that our producers can actually sell their products abroad.
The producers of military products and capital projects have another Crown corporation, the Canadian Commercial Corporation, which provides them specific assistance in implementing projects abroad. This sector that is not making the same kind of wholesome contribution is favoured by government assistance in marketing its products.
The need for Canagrex was recognized because the agricultural community had no instrument available to it that could provide assistance in attacking the complex world of international trade. It was apparent that the agricultural community, considered by some to be the least sophisticated in looking beyond Canada's borders for foreign markets, needed expertise
Canagrex
and financial instruments to open up new opportunities for its very excellent producers, who needed to widen their markets so they could get their products sold. This would have reversed the trade deficit in non-grain agricultural products.
The Minister of Agriculture at the time Canagrex was brought in, the Hon. Eugene Whelan, had held the portfolio for some 12 years and had recognized very soon after his appointment that Canada had not recognized its potential as a bread-basket of the world. In the late 1970s, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture complained about missed opportunities for Canadian producers in export markets. It was also seen that most other major agricultural exporting nations had organizations as part of their Governments or created by their Governments to provide export assistance in agriculture.
Seeing what other countries were doing and recognizing pressure from the producers, Canada finally moved in the late 1970s and eventually in 1981, brought Canagrex in for approval. We were finally starting to give our farmers the kind of assistance that other countries were giving theirs.
I can see that my time is just about up. I want to register very clearly my opposition and that of my Party to this very precipitous move on the part of the Government to chop Canagrex before it has had a chance to prove itself in a concerted way, and after initial reports of its success have shown that it was making a contribution. In fact, it was acting as producers had hoped it would. It was acting as an advocate for agriculture. I will certainly be opposing the Government's move to shut down this agency that our producers very much need.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Questions and comments.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great attention to the speech of the Hon. Member. I want to compliment her for speaking so eloquently about this erroneous initiative on the part of the Tories. It is not the first time they have been wrong-headed, as you know, being the objective person you are.
The Tories want to abolish Canagrex at a time when there has been an onslaught of farm subsidies by the U.S. It comes at a time when the U.S. is taking a particular initiative, one we do not like, in assisting its farmers in the export market. I am thinking of the provisions of the U.S. Farm Bill, specifically designed to displace the exports of other countries. This has the effect of lowering commodity prices for our farmers. At the same time our Government is embarking on another wrong-headed initiative, the free trade negotiations.
Given all that, would it not be more appropriate for the Tories to support Canagrex in order to increase our multilateral trade and ensure that we do not become even more dependent upon the U.S. than we are now? We would have some ability to defend ourselves when the U.S., or any other country for that matter, brings in the kind of initiatives we see in the

September 11, 1987
Canagrex
U.S. Farm Bill which amount to some $70 billion worth of subsidies to displace the exports of other countries.
Would the Hon. Member not agree that the Government would be far better advised to dp that rather than take this approach which has lost them support both federally and provincially, as we saw last night?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member raises a number of extremely important questions in his remarks. I share the suspicion of many people that the abolition of Canagrex is perhaps one offering by the Conservative Party to the Americans in order to obtain a free trade deal. The Government likes to say it is not, but of course we are not in the room when these things are discussed so we cannot verify it one way or another.
Pursuing a trade deal with the U.S. will mean we will be dominated even more by the American economy. The U.S. is already our major trading partner and probably will be for the foreseeable future, but we would like to see more multilateral trade and a diversification of our export markets. Canagrex would have been part of that diversification. In a sense it is needed now more than ever.
The Hon. Member referred to the mass of subsidies to American producers. While Canagrex by itself cannot cope with that kind of situation, it would at least help our farmers market their products around the world. We need to be diversifying into new markets and Canagrex would help us achieve that goal.

Mr. Speaker, 1 represent an urban constituency but I feel it important that I speak on this issue because so many of the people I represent work for the railways or work in the plants which produce agricultural machinery. Their well-being is to a large extent dependent upon the well-being of the farmers they serve.
I could not help but be surprised by the laughter from the Conservative benches when my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), spoke in support of this Bill. It seems to me that our Conservative friends will never learn, no matter what happens to them. Given the disaster they suffered yesterday in the Province of Ontario where they went from governing that province for more than 40 years to being the third Party, surely they should have realized that the people have demonstrated that they do not accept the Conservative philosophy that the best Government is a Government that does the least; just let the free enterprise system operate without interference or direction by Government and everything will be fine according to the Conservatives. Surely they should have learned from yesterday's election, as they will learn in the soon to be held New Brunswick election, that the people of Canada do not accept that principle and are not going to support a Party which endorses it.
We are not living in paradise. We are not living in some theoretical world. The facts of life are that almost every country, whether it has a Government of the supposed right or
left, has intervened very substantially to help its agricultural sector. Whether it be the U.S., France, Germany, Great Britain or Japan, to mention just a few of the major countries, it is realized that the free enterprise system does not always work in ways which help people. For that reason they have all become involved in a variety of ways, through tariffs, quotas or the extension of cheap credit, in plans to help their people.
Let us look just at agriculture. The world is producing more food than it ever did before and we have more hungry people. It has been estimated that there are at least 500 million hungry people in the world. We have great food surpluses, not because people do not need the food but because many of those people cannot afford to buy it.
The agricultural sector of our economy is in great trouble. When our grain farmers can sell their grain they are selling it at the lowest prices we have seen since the hungry thirties. They are taking a loss on every bushel of grain they sell. Our fruit farmers, vegetable farmers and dairy farmers are all in great difficulty, not because they are not efficient and cannot produce a high quality product but because of the support given to farmers of other countries.
The Americans have taken over markets which Canada has had for many years by subsidizing the price of grain to their farmers. The European Economic Community has mountains of butter because it has subsidized the production of it as it has beef and many other products. That is the situation our farmers have to face.
It is not as though our governments, federal and provincial, have followed the free market approach in the field of agriculture. We have marketing boards and agencies at both levels established over the years by Liberal, Conservative, NDP, Parti Quebecois and Social Credit governments. Most of those governments believed in a free enterprise system but realized that the reality of life for agricultural producers is that we need forms of supply management if farmers are to continue to produce and not have to cut back on their standard of living or declare bankruptcy, as thousands, if not tens of thousands, of them have done.
Canagrex was one of the few good ideas brought forward by the former Liberal Government. It was a way of helping Canadian farmers sell their products on the export markets. That proposal received the support of a number of the major farm organizations in this country. The President of the National Farmers Union, Mr. Wayne Easter, said in a statement issued March 14, 1985:
The Canadian farmer for which Canagrex was established deserves better, and the federal government's unwillingness to consult either the industry or Canagrex officials prior to the November 8/84 announcement by the Minister of Agriculture is nothing more than a slap in the face to farmers across Canada.
He was talking, of course, about the announcement by the Conservative Government that it proposed to do away with Canagrex.
September 11, 1987

The Saskatchewan Wheat Pool and the Manitoba Wheat Pool, which represent a majority of the grain farmers in those two provinces, have spoken up in favour of the establishment and continued operation of Canagrex.
We must ask ourselves why the Government is doing this. It is doing it, as 1 have indicated, in part because of its fixation with the idea that the free enterprise system and getting government out of the running of the economy as much as possible is a fundamental part of its principle? Another reason was mentioned by my colleague from Broadview-Greenwood. She talked about the insane desire and determination of the Conservative Government to press ahead for a free trade agreement with the United States on almost any terms.
Last night on The National, after quite a bit of time spent relating the disaster which the Conservatives suffered in the Ontario election, we heard some news from Washington. In answer to a question from Republican Senator Lugar of Indiana and the American Secretary of State, George Shultz, made it very clear that the United States would not agree, in a free trade agreement with Canada, to give up the power which the American Congress has to countervail. What kind of free trade agreement will we have if every time some American industry believes it is being hurt by Canadian competition it can put on a tariff?
We need only look at the Province of Saskatchewan. There was no stronger supporter of free trade than Conservative Premier Devine of Saskatchewan. When the producers of potash in New Mexico said that they could not compete with the much more efficient potash industry in Saskatchewan a tariff of 68 per cent, if my memory is correct, was suddenly imposed.
That great defender of free trade, Mr. Devine, then brought in legislation which no federal or provincial government in Canada has ever before brought forward. I am not being critical. I am not sure he made the right decision, but he realized he had to take very drastic action to protect that industry which has sales of several billion dollars a year and employs 4,000 Saskatchewan workers. This approach to free trade is another illustration of the absolute irresponsibility and stupidity of the Conservative Government.
Some may have thought that Canagrex, which was established by the Liberal Government with the approval of the NDP and the initial approval at least of the Conservatives, would eliminate the private sector and interfere with the ability of the private companies involved in the grain, beef or pork industries to continue to operate as they always have. Nothing could be further from the truth. The role of Canagrex was simply to help the Canadian producers of grain, pork, beef and tobacco, and the companies involved in those industries, to make sales overseas. It was beginning to play a very useful and important role until the Government, in its mad insistence on
the free enterprise system, decided that Canagrex should be abolished.
Mr. Speaker, it is 11 o'clock.

subsubtopic: PLEA ON BEHALF OF IRIS PADILLA MASON
speechtext:
Today, Mr. Speaker, I have a request to make to the Minister responsible for citizenship. I am referring to Mrs. Iris Padilla Mason who was born in Santiago, Chile, who taught for 20 years, and who was imprisoned in 1974.
On the occasion of the international Liberal meeting she came to make representations this morning and to tell us how she had been victimized, but also to ask for her Canadian citizenship. She first came to Canada in 1976 as a refugee and then became an immigrant, but she has been unable to obtain her citizenship papers. She told us that for two years now she has been making every attempt to become a Canadian citizen but that the Department has failed to respond.
I therefore urge the Minister responsible for citizenship-I know he gives due consideration to such requests!-to pay particular attention to the case of Mrs. Iris Padilla Mason.

Mr. Speaker, the appreciation of the House of Commons ought to be extended to the police forces of Toronto, Montreal and Ottawa who have co-operated successfully to break up a juvenile prostitution ring which was operating in those cities.
The very idea of child prostitution is abhorrent to Canadians, and adults who lure children into the practice and then live off the avails should be dealt with as forcefully as the law allows. Since many of the young people involved in this particular case were wards of the Children's Aid Society, perhaps there is a need to review our system of child welfare.

September 11, 1987

maintopic: S. O. 21 HEALTH IRRADIATION OF FOOD-COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATIONS

speechtext:
Mir. Nelson A. Riis (Kamloops-Shuswap): Mr. Speaker, the committee investigating the irradiation of food in Canada studied the issue for many months. It received many briefs and held hearings in Ottawa and other parts of Canada.
The evidence which they examined included over 800 studies of the food irradiation issue. The overwhelming majority of those studies either opposed food irradiation or were neutral in terms of posing all sorts of unanswered questions regarding the irradiation of food. Those very few in favour tended to be linked in some way to the nuclear industry.
After hard work in a non-partisan atmosphere, the committee made important recommendations to the Minister and the Government regarding what it should do in terms of food irradiation. Yesterday, the Minister essentially turned his back on the recommendations and has ignored them all.
At a time when states in the U.S. are passing legislation to ban the irradiation of food and when other countries are looking into it and seriously considering similar steps, Canada appears to be moving ahead. I urge the Minister to consider the recommendations of the committee and accept them.

subtopic: OPENING OF UNITED WAY CAMPAIGN IN OTTAWA-CARLETON
OPENING OF UNITED WAY CAMPAIGN IN OTTAWA-CARLETON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning, together with my colleagues, the Member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Turner), the Member for Ottawa West (Mr. Daubney), and the Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy), I attended a breakfast with 1,000 volunteers to kick off the United Way campaign in Ottawa-Carleton. This year the goal is some $9.2 million in support of 70 programs delivered through 48 agencies.
The United Way is a volunteer non-profit organization that pulls our community together. It matches the human care needs with our resources through one annual fund-raising drive. Volunteers determine its standards, direction, and priorities.
Mr. Speaker, I welcomed your recent endorsement of the United Way campaign among employees who work for Parliament.
Similar campaigns will be starting all across Canada. As Members of Parliament, I urge each of us to recognize their importance and to support this most valuable program in our towns and cities across the nation.

Prescott-Russell): Mr. Speaker, yesterday the people of Ontario gave this province its first majority Liberal Government in 50 years. They did so with a resounding majority. maintopic: TRIBUTE TO HULL ATHLETE, MICHEL CAREAU
TRIBUTE TO HULL ATHLETE, MICHEL CAREAU
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour for me to draw the attention of the House to a major and notable achievement which has received very little publicity in Canada, except from the sports media. Last June, Hull athlete Michel Careau accumulated more miles in an organized race than any other Canadian marathoner or ultramarathoner. In fact, he came in second in the New York race, which puts him in second place among the best runners in the world over very long distances. Only three runners have succeeded in breaking the psychological 1,000-mile barrier in a race against the clock: The winner, Marty Sprengelmeyer of the United States, Michel Careau of Canada in second place, and Dan Coffey of Britain in third place.
Mr. Careau, a senior public servant at the federal Department of National Health and Welfare, often takes part in races held for charity and humanitarian causes. Last August 8, he made a speech on peace at the United Nations on the occasion of an international race for peace held in 57 countries.
Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to join with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), who is very proud and happy to have Mr. Michel Careau on his team, in paying a public tribute to this great Canadian who brings us honour, not only in Canada, but everywhere he goes to run against the best known athletes in the sport of long distance running.
September 11, 1987

Mr. Speaker, the Post Office's policy of franchising rural post offices is not only causing a loss of service in rural Canada, it is also bringing about drastic cuts in income for rural post office employees.
If that is not enough to call this policy into question, we must keep in mind the fact that 80 per cent of post office workers in rural Canada are women.
Will the Government continue the policy of asking women to subsidize Canadian society unfairly? Will it fight the deficit in the Post Office on the backs of women who, in some cases, are being asked to have their wages cut by one-fifth? It is time for this injustice to stop.
It is time to question the policy of franchising when, rather than achieve equality, it increases inequality for women in our society.

subtopic: INFORMATION AND POPULARIZATION EFFORT FOR UPCOMING GENERATION
INFORMATION AND POPULARIZATION EFFORT FOR UPCOMING GENERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week, the Young Farmers' Regional Centre of the Lac-Saint-Jean constituency launched the game "Defi-Releve".
The purpose of this game is to make players aware of the difficulties of farming. It also provides information on the farming relief groups in Quebec and explains the work of the farmer, in addition to promoting dialogue in farming families and educating people who are not familiar with farming.
I wish to underline the information and popularization effort this game represents.
The farming community is of vital importance for Canada and it is essential for the whole population to know something about it, and I believe that this game can contribute to this end. Congratulations on this initiative!

Both as a Canadian and Francophone Quebecer, Mr. Speaker, I am proud of the choice Ontario people made yesterday. I am
proud not because they elected Liberals-that is for sure-but because they rejected all those who opposed bilingualism. They rejected outright and unquestionably all those men and women who would not progress with the Canadian people as a whole. You can rest assured that as a Francophone Quebecer, I am proud and I congratulate my federal colleagues from Ontario, as well as the people from Ontario for their choice. As the Honourable Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) was saying, the Ontario people have heard the message of such pioneers as the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier and the Hon. Member for Glengarrry-Prescott-Russell who have fought for the Francophone minority. I think that as Quebecers, we can be proud to have remained in Canada!

Mr. Speaker, of the many reasons for the Mulroney Government's unpopularity, one reason must surely be because of its continued efforts to automate Canada's lightstations in order to end the long tradition of service performed by our nation's lightkeepers. This week the government-appointed Leblond review on the impact of destaffing the B.C. lightstations concluded: "Sufficient evidence has been found to conclude that a human presence is not absolutely necessary to keep lights and foghorns functioning at a satisfactory level of reliability".
While this view may agree with the continued wish of the Mulroney Government to eliminate important services wherever and whenever possible, it is not the view of ordinary British Columbians. The British Columbians who sail our coast have spoken with one voice against any further decrease in marine safety and against the elimination of lightkeepers.
Lightkeepers have logged hundreds upon hundreds of hours of lifesaving search and rescue work, work that could never be done by a machine. No one but this Government has been willing to suggest that lightkeepers are a waste of money and that their functions should be automated.
One month from now the Coast Guard will table its final plans for de-staffing West Coast lightstations. As long as the reliability of automated equipment remains in doubt, as long as lightkeepers continue to deliver an important service to our nation's mariners, the Government must give up its life-threatening policy of ignoring the needs of our coastal residents.
No more closures. No more reductions. British Columbians say that today and they will say it again in the next election.

September 11, 1987

maintopic: CALL FOR PASSAGE OF BILL C-22 TO AMEND PATENT ACT
CALL FOR PASSAGE OF BILL C-22 TO AMEND PATENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the unelected Senate has decided to stall Bill C-22 by referring it to its Senate Committee on Banking, Trade and Commerce. I agree the Senate does have a role to play, but by sending Bill C-22 back the first time with amendments, it has already utilized its powers. It has not been elected by Canadians to be the Government, and by repeating its tactics it just serves to prove that changes must be made to the Upper Chamber.
The facts are clear. The same committee, which is now going to examine the legislation, refused to pre-study it last November 28. After more than 150 hours of Senate debate, there is now nothing further to study or review. This legislation has also received more time in debate in our Chamber than any other Bill this session.
The Senate is jeopardizing at least 3,000 jobs and $1.4 billion in investment. By its first delay alone, companies which had announced plans to expand operations pending the passage of Bill C-22 have now had to put their plans on hold. Universities and teaching hospitals were also counting on the millions of dollars in promised new research funds for this fall's curricula and programs. They must now wait longer.
This Government was elected by the majority of Canadians who want research and development to grow in Canada. The Senate does not have the support of any one in this country to continue stalling Bill C-22. It does not even have the support of its Leader, the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner). I call on Members of the other Chamber to come to their senses and pass Bill C-22.

subtopic: VISIT TO CANADA BY HEAD OF CHINA WELFARE FUND FOR THE HANDICAPPED
VISIT TO CANADA BY HEAD OF CHINA WELFARE FUND FOR THE HANDICAPPED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, next week Deng Pufang, the son of Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping, is visiting Canada. I would like to welcome him to Canada. This is an important visit. Mr. Deng is the Director General of the China Welfare Fund for the Handicapped. He himself is handicapped. He is confined to a wheelchair after being crippled when he was thrown out of an upper-storey window at Beijing University during the excesses of the Cultural Revolution. He is returning to Ottawa where he was treated in the Ottawa Civic Hospital.
Our relations with China are very important. I think it will be the country of the 21st Century, along with Canada. We have made great progress in Canada, particularly in the House of Commons, with our facilities for the handicapped in the last couple of years. Let us show Mr. Deng the progress we have
made. Let us co-operate with the Chinese so we can perhaps give to them some of the ideas we have developed, and they can use them in their own country where there are 20 million handicapped people.

subtopic: INCREASE IN NUMBER OF HELP-WANTED ADVERTISEMENTS
INCREASE IN NUMBER OF HELP-WANTED ADVERTISEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was surprised this morning to learn that StatsCan keeps an index on help-wanted ads. However, I was not surprised to learn what that index shows. For the fourth month in a row the number of help-wanted ads in Canada has increased. That shows there are jobs around. In Ontario we are having difficulty filling construction jobs and jobs in the service industry. There is a prosperity in Canada that began September 4, 1984, when this Government was elected.
Our Leader was laughed at for promising "jobs, jobs, jobs". What a laugh for a million jobs! Our prosperity will continue as long as we have the good management of this Government. I know the confidence of all Canadians has been restored with respect to investment in Canada.

subtopic: NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY'S POLICY ON USE OF VIOLENCE IN AFRICA
NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY'S POLICY ON USE OF VIOLENCE IN AFRICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the Ottawa Citizen this morning there is a Canadian Press article which states:
The New Democratic Party's external affairs spokesman said Thursday her
Party supports the use of violence by black Africans as a way to end South
Africa's apartheid regime.
You know, Mr. Speaker, that I spent many years living and working in east and central Africa. I have travelled throughout most of Commonwealth Africa. I ask you, Sir, the question: is violence the key to the solution in Uganda, Chad, Zaire or the Sudan? It is certainly not the key to the solution, and it is also not the key to the solution in Central America where there is tremendous violence going on.
The Hon. Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett) went on to say that sometimes a resort to violence is absolutely essential in the struggle. That may be true, but to endorse violence in the House of Commons of Canada is completely barbaric and unacceptable. This comes from the Party that wanted to invade St. Pierre and Miquelon, that wanted to bring in the gunboats and go to war with France over the fishing disagreement between Newfoundland and Canada. That is absolutely unbelievable. It calls itself the
September 11, 1987

Party of the common people. Pretty soon it is going to be inciting violence in Canada against some policies of the Government of Canada.
Now I know why the New Democrats want to pull out of NATO and NORAD and bring the troops home, because they are going to incite violence in Canada because they disagree with some of the things we as the Government are doing. This is unbelievable.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: SOUTH AFRICA-USE OF VIOLENCE-SEVERANCE OF DIPLOMATIC RELATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. The Conservative position on South Africa is all over the map, and I want to give the Government another opportunity to come clean with Canadians. The Prime Minister, to the great applause of the United Nations at the session two years ago, promised total economic sanctions. He promised a breach of diplomatic relations if the situation continued to deteriorate.

subsubtopic: SOUTH AFRICA-USE OF VIOLENCE-SEVERANCE OF DIPLOMATIC RELATIONS
speechtext: Take a stand today. Don't wimp out.

subsubtopic: SOUTH AFRICA-USE OF VIOLENCE-SEVERANCE OF DIPLOMATIC RELATIONS
speechtext:
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has taken a different position. He did impose some sanctions. He now says that sanctions are not the answer. Yet he admits that Canada believes that the situation in South Africa is deteriorating.
I heard an interjection from my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap. The official position of the New Democratic Party on South Africa is dangerous. The NDP says that severing diplomatic relations with South Africa would be too harsh, yet it supports violence as a solution.
Does the Government reject violence out of hand as a solution to the South Africa problem? And when will the Prime Minister get the Government's act together, fulfil the commitment made to the United Nations, and advance the case in Vancouver that there must be total diplomatic sanctions and there has to be a breach of diplomatic relations, on a firm schedule?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: SOUTH AFRICA-USE OF VIOLENCE-SEVERANCE OF DIPLOMATIC RELATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the position articulated by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition is, in my judgment, calculated to achieve headlines in Canada rather than progress in South Africa.
What we are attempting to do is to continue to build pressure for change, pressure upon the South African Government to bring an end to the apartheid regime. We have been able to use Canada's influence constructively in that regard at
Oral Questions
Nassau, and at the Venice Summit. We expect to be able to contribute substantially and significantly to that process at the Heads of Government meeting in Vancouver.
With regard to the position concerning violence, I made that position clear yesterday in response to the NDP endorsement of violence.

subtopic: VIOLATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS OF BLACK AFRICANS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: VIOLATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS OF BLACK AFRICANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister received his share of favourable headlines two years ago when he made his speech in the United Nations to which I referred.
I met with Oliver Tambo recently, and the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Prime Minister had their own meeting with him. Mr. Tambo did not ask me to have Canada provide military aid to the front-line states, nor did he ask Canada to encourage violence. What he asked our country for was an imposition of total economic sanctions and for a breach of diplomatic relations. The Prime Minister said he would impose such sanctions, both economically and diplomatically, if the situation deteriorated.
The prime and moral issue for the world is that the human rights of 26 million black Africans are being violated and trampled upon year by year, month by month, and day by day.
Therefore, why has the Prime Minister reversed the position he advanced on behalf of Canada at the United Nations, and why is the Government not fulfilling that commitment?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: VIOLATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS OF BLACK AFRICANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I say, with all affection for the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition, that if he wishes to improve his standing in the country, he should choose some other issue. The charge he is making against the Prime Minister is not only false, but it is known to be false across this country and, more important, it is known to be false across and throughout Africa.
Under this Prime Minister the constructive role that Canada has played in attempting to build effective pressure against South Africa to bring about an end to apartheid is understood, for example, by President Houphouet-Boigny of Cote d'Ivoire, it is understood by President Kenneth Kaunda of Zambia, and it is understood by President Chissano of Mozambique. It is understood in the front-line states throughout Africa.
They may not understand the imperative of a Canadian politician seeking headlines at home, but they understand and applaud what Canada is doing internationally.

The House was recalled as a matter of emergency this summer to consider two Bills, C-84 and C-85, in order to put an end to so-called immigration abuses. They have been considered and passed. Everyone says that in the Georges Grossmann case, there were three interventions-one at least from the Minister's office, and another one from the Prime Minister's Office, to speed up matters and have Mr. Grossmann's application jump the line.

subsubtopic: GROSSMANN AFFAIR-REQUEST FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, again let me categorically repudiate those allegations of impropriety or illegality which I have clearly set out this week.
Over 7,000 letters are received by my office. There are criteria under which certain concerns may be considered, usually on humanitarian and compassionate conditions. In Mr. Grossmann's case I will again clearly lay out what took place for those who were not with us yesterday.
In January a letter was referred to my office for our attention. In the month of May I decided to proceed with inland processing by asking that the Deputy Minister see that a Minister's permit was issued. From then on nothing further has to be done on my part, it is a routine and normal processing. I do not follow it up. I know that all goes well. I know that this takes place over 15,000 times a year, 99 per cent of the time by officials who advance such a permit.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
On that issue I side with Renaud Paquet, the president of the union, who stated yesterday that "when we receive a letter from the Prime Minister's Office it has more impact than a letter that is received from anybody else". My question to the Minister-

speechtext: Is he no longer a Member of Parliament? Is that what you are saying? You have got to be crazy.

Why does the Minister not follow the recommendations of the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Immigration who stated yesterday that he feels the whole matter should be referred to the committee for study and consideration? Why does he not follow the advice of his own Member?

Mr. Speaker, yesterday I tabled the guidelines for conditions under which we are able to act. I guess I have already given the answer, and it is no use repeating what I said.
Clearly we have a case here where the individual has been in the country for over six years, employment authorizations had been renewed each time for six consecutive years, his longterm prospects are good in the country, and he has a son who is apparently married to a Canadian who could have sponsored him. Everything to do with this case was completely normal. It
September 11, 1987

took us four months of review, and that is how we had to act in a very appropriate fashion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to return to the issue of free trade with the United States. With respect to a mandate, and just as a preamble to my question, I should like to ask the Hon. Minister how she can say that there is a mandate for free trade when it was not mentioned during the last election and her Leader campaigned against it when he sought the leadership of his Party.
In particular, is it not correct that Secretary of State Shultz said that any dispute settlement mechanism with his country will have to be consistent with United States trade laws?
How can there be a dispute settlement mechanism whose rulings are binding on both countries and still be consistent with American trade laws? Is he not clearly telling the Government that a supposed key condition for a free trade deal simply is not on? Is this not a signal that there is no deal unless the Government is going to cave in on this key demand?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pat Carney (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext:
No,
Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if there have already been signals from key American Senators and from Secretary of State Shultz that this supposed key demand by the Government for a mechanism whose rulings will be binding on both Governments in trade disputes is unacceptable, why is the Minister continuing these talks when it is clear that these talks will lead to a result which will not be in the best interests of Canada and contrary to the needs of Canadians on jobs and sovereignty? Why is she continuing on this path without any real mandate from the Canadian people?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pat Carney (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when the Government ran for office successfully we ran on the mandate of creating jobs, and we have been very successful in that issue. We will shortly be creating the millionth job since the Government took office.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Do you have one for Mr. Grossman?

May I point out that the free trade initiative is about jobs; that is what it is. It is about jobs in all regions of the country. The Economic Council of Canada has estimated that there will be 350,000 new jobs created by this initiative and that, in the absence of it, Canadians stand to lose jobs because of protectionism in the United States.
Our mandate comes from our promise to create jobs, and we are delivering on that mandate.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Immigration and concerns the Grossmann issue-

subsubtopic: GRANTING OF LANDED IMMIGRANT STATUS-INVOLVEMENT OF OFFICIALS
speechtext:
The immigration issue. Yesterday the Minister left a very crucial question unanswered. The Minister stated that this was a very simple, straightforward, and routine immigration case. As a matter of fact he stated that again today, as he has on a number of occasions.
If that is the case, would the Minister then explain to the House, and to the people of Canada who are very interested in the issue, why it was that every senior immigration officer in the country, from the Prime Minister's Office down, was involved in it? subsubtopic: GRANTING OF LANDED IMMIGRANT STATUS-INVOLVEMENT OF OFFICIALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what is very simple and straightforward is that on May 4 I indicate my intention by Minister's permit to advance inland processing. I do that by asking the Deputy Minister to carry through with the process. I do not follow up what procedures may then take place. That is not for me to do. That is technical.
Perhaps the Hon. Member has not had a complete briefing on how the Immigration Department functions, but we know that everything goes well following my asking the Deputy Minister to do what is my intention.
It is a normal part of immigration processing. As I said, almost 16,000 times a year this is carried on. I only wish that the Hon. Member and others would not try to confuse the issue with other issues that may be on the table dealing with the arrival of illegal migrants in the country.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Immigration. Write Mila.

Mr. Speaker, we are certainly very aware of the arrival of the increasing number of Hondurans, more particularly on the West Coast. We are monitoring the situation very carefully.
My information is that more than 1,000 have now come to make a refugee claim in Canada. It is part of the increasing abuse and I say this without trying to predispose whether these people may be refugees or not because I do not make that determination.
The Hon. Member has seen a Government that has now been bombarded with an increasing flow of refugee claimants. The advice that I have been getting from my Refugee Status Advisory Committee is that almost 90 per cent of them are non-bona fide claimants. It is for that reason that, once and for all, this House should get on with the business of passing Bill C-55 and putting in place a refugee determination process that makes sense, that balances fairness with compassion and will offer genuine protection to those who need it. subsubtopic: REQUEST ON BEHALF OF REFUGEE FAMILY FROM CHILE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State who is responsible for the granting of citizenship. This morning, in the presence of Liberal International, the National Women's Liberal Commission adopted the cause of the family of Iris Mason, a family which has arrived from Chile and has landed immigrant status. This family came from Chile where its members suffered horrible oppression and torture. They have been refused Canadian citizenship by the Government on national security grounds.
The family members appealed to the Security Intelligence Review Committee which recommended that they be given citizenship, but the Government has still refused. I gave the Secretary of State notice of my question which follows.
In light of the tragic circumstances which brought the Mason family to Canada will he accept the advice of the Government's own review committee and grant Canadian citizenship?

subsubtopic: REQUEST ON BEHALF OF REFUGEE FAMILY FROM CHILE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, let me thank the Hon. Member for being in touch with my office just prior to Question Period. It allowed me the opportunity to call for the file. I will take the opportunity to read it over the weekend, and I invite the Hon. Member to meet with me on Monday morning.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for Multiculturalism; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think it is important that what I do is review the file before any action is taken. I am sure the Hon. Member understands that. I have not seen the file. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Recently Mr. Fortier, the Canadian negotiator with the French on the fish talks, was in Newfoundland and consulted with the Government of Newfoundland. The position of the Newfoundland Government is very clear. Northern cod is not to be begged, borrowed or stolen. Mr. Fortier would not comment one way or the other on that position.
What is the position of the Government of Canada in view of the importance of that resource to the fishermen of Newfoundland and to Atlantic Canada? Is northern cod on the table? Is it to be bargained away to the French?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the position of the Government of Canada is that this is a matter that has to be negotiated between Canada and France. As a result of a meeting between Prime Minister Chirac and the Prime Minister of Canada, negotiations were opened again. They had been cut off by the French but they are opened again and will begin tomorrow in Paris.
As we have committed regularly in the House, any negotiations by Canada will involve continuous consultation with the interested parties including, the Province of Newfoundland. Those consultations will occur. Representatives of the Province of Newfoundland and other groups will be present as part of the Canadian delegation involved in the negotiations.
I do not propose to publish in the House of Commons the negotiating position Canada will take into the discussions with France tomorrow. To do that would be to jeopardize the Canadian and Newfoundland position. I would not want to do that.

speakeroldname: Hon. William Rompkey (Grand Falls-White Bay- Labrador):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I repeat that the position of the Newfoundland Government is very clear. Not only that, but yesterday the Minister of Fisheries in Newfoundland, the poorest province in Canada, put up $1 million to alleviate the crisis in the inshore fishery.
How can the Government of Canada allocate billions of dollars to protect Canadian sovereignty in the North and at the same time give away, propose to give away, or allow to give away the most important northern resource we have which is northern cod? How can he justify that?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs

Mr. Speaker, the premise, of course, is false. We are dealing with the problem. We have a negotiation under way now because the earlier arrangement put in place by a Government of which the Hon. Member was a part was insufficient. It did not provide adequate protection for Canada. It left a problem that must be resolved by negotiations. We are carrying out those negotiations now.
In the past when negotiations were carried out by Liberal Governments, the provinces and other interested parties were excluded. We have changed that practice. We have brought the Province of Newfoundland, other provinces and other interested groups into the consultation and the delegation for the negotiation. That is what is happening with regard to the negotiations in Paris this weekend and I make the commitment that we will be protecting the Canadian and the Newfoundland interests in those negotiations.
September 11, 1987

Would the Minister tell us why this unfairness exists? Individuals who would like to lobby in favour of a health Bill, be it Bill C-51 or Bill C-204, do not get any tax advantages whatsoever and charities risk losing their charitable status if they spend more than 10 per cent of their money on advocacy. Why is there this anomaly? Will he do something about that unfairness?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member realizes that these rules and regulations are put in place for a purpose. The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Wise that Bill C-2, an Act to dissolve Canagrex and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof, be read the third time and passed.

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of establishing Canagrex was not to interfere with private sector operations in this industry, it was not to hurt it but to help it. I would like to put on the record some of the comments of the President and Chief Executive Officer of Canagrex, Mr. A. E. Story, when he appeared before the House of Commons Standing Committee on Agriculture on March 11, 1985. He said in part as follows:
Immediately upon opening the offices of Canagrex on January 3rd, 1984, we set about preparing a corporate plan which was later approved by our board of directors and signed by the Minister of Agriculture. It was my firm intention to carry out the corporate plan and operate the corporation based upon private sector principles. I hired the most results-oriented people I could find.
He said further:
The suggestions expressed by many of the agricultural associations and industry groups such as the Canadian Exporters Association were very helpful.
In other words, he consulted with them. He said further:
Concern was often expressed that we would exercise the powers in the Canagrex Act to undertake direct buying and selling. We were determined that we would leave the buying and selling to the private sector. We did not interfere in the marketplace.
Mr. Story went on to explain what they were doing and said:
We prepared a survey of Canadian commodities available for export. This source list of Canadian commodities is probably the most comprehensive and up-to-date available anywhere today.
Surely we have the right to ask why other departments did not prepare such a list. Why did the Department of Agriculture not do it? Why destroy the organization which prepared this very important list? He continued:
We developed a market survey program. This entailed in-depth research on specific market areas which we considered as potentially promising and most interested in buying Canadian products.

September 11, 1987
Canagrex
He went on to illustrate what he meant. He said:
For example, we had a pork producer accompany our mission to Singapore, we had a potato producer travel with us to Cuba. We also had tobacco producers travel with our group to Egypt, Hungary and Czechoslovakia, where we initiated the negotiation process to assist in selling to these markets.
The valuable market information which we gathered was fed back to the Canadian industry.
Why would the Government put a stop to that kind of valuable assistance?
He continued:
We undertook a program to stimulate export sales abroad. For example, Canagrex defrayed some of the cost involved in transporting high quality breeding swine to Italy on the understanding that out of any subsequent sales, Canagrex would recover their expenses. As it turned out, the Canadian swine won several medals at the Milano exhibition. As a result of these efforts, foreign buyers visited Canada to investigate further purchases of Canadian swine.
Farmers in my province of Manitoba produce a substantial number of pigs and would like to expand their production. However, there is no use expanding production if they cannot make sales. If Canagrex could help sell more swine in Italy, why would the Conservative Government destroy it? Mr. Story said further:
The Buyers Credit Guarantee Program was an important area of Canagrex operations. We sought to have the risks shared among the Canadian exporters, the banks or the insurance companies and the foreign buyer. A Canagrex guarantee was provided when it was deemed absolutely necessary.
That is what all the other governments are doing. They help their producers by providing loans at low interest rates and providing subsidies. They do everything they can to help their producers. Surely to God, given the tremendous difficulties which Canadian producers of agricultural products are facing, we should be doing everything we can. Instead, blinded by the Government's mystic belief in the free market, its opposition to government involvement, and its belief that the best government is the government which does the least, the Government has taken the completely irresponsible and wrong decision to destroy Canagrex.
We intend to vote against this Bill for all the reasons which I and other members of the New Democratic Party have listed. We believe that the establishment of Canagrex was a good idea. It made a good start and should have been helped to expand its activities rather than being destroyed as it will be when this Bill is passed.

Mr. Speaker, in its annual report Canagrex indicated that it was having difficulty getting backing from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in order to provide financing for the exporting of a number of different agricultural products. It had asked the Ministry of Finance for a global figure beyond which it could not provide financing by way of export guarantees. The Ministry of Finance kept dragging its feet and refusing that financing until finally the Minister of Finance, in his first financial statement to the House, indicated that the Government had made a decision to do away with Canagrex.
Does the Hon. Member believe that the idea of the Minister of Finance was to make the performance of Canagrex's functions as difficult as possible by inaction on approving the export financing arrangements which the Act provided for Canagrex?

Mr. Speaker, I can, of course, only speculate on the thinking of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). However, he did to Canagrex what he had done in so many other cases. The Minister of Finance is so fixed with the need to reduce the deficit that he would not give Canagrex the go-ahead by giving it the money it needed. He did the same thing in the field of scientific research which, of course, includes agricultural research. I have never heard such devastating criticism of a Minister of Finance as I did in the documents released recently by the Canadian Association of University Teachers, who go into great detail about how the cut-backs in funding have hurt scientific research. The refusal of the Minister of Finance to supply the funds for Canagrex is just part and parcel of his whole approach that he must cut the deficit, regardless of the very serious and adverse effects it has on Canagrex and ail other government organizations which need adequate financing.
