PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE SHIPBUILDING INDUSTRY THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A REVITALIZATION SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That a special committee of this House be established to consider the problems affecting the shipbuilding industry, with a view to initiating a revitalization of that industry in Quebec.
He said: First, Mr. Speaker, I want to explain why this committee should be established. Let it be known from the outset that I would be prepared to accept an amendment motion if the Government wanted to extend the committee's terms of reference to the whole country. I am convinced that my colleague from Saint-Maurice (Mr. Grondin) would support this amendment because I think that Quebec's shipbuilding industry problems have a similar impact in the Maritime Provinces, in Ontario, and in Western Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out why.. . Hon. Members will recall that before the 1984 election the previous Liberal administration used to spread contracts around to make sure that none of Canada's shipyards would remain idle.
We have three major shipyards in Quebec: Lauzon near Quebec City, Sorel, and Vickers in Montreal. Back in 1984, before the election brought the Conservative Government to power, these three shipyards had landed contracts-frigates for the Montreal and Sorel shipyards, and a contract for the Caribou ferry which had been awarded to Lauzon's shipyards. However, there had been a transaction in the meantime. The owners of the Lauzon shipyard purchased the Montreal shipyard, and without the agreement of the Government and without advising anyone, transferred all the Montreal contracts to the Lauzon shipyard in Quebec City, which could have meant the closing of the Vickers shipyard in Montreal,
Shipbuilding
which shipyard had historically provided jobs and enjoyed a certain influence.
We all recall the lethargic attitude of the Conservative Government in the case of the Gulf refinery and of Bombardier. Then, we had the announcement of the closing of this shipyard and of several businesses and the loss of 5,000 jobs. With the provincial and federal representatives of East Montreal, I created a survival committee to force the Conservative Government to take action on these issues, stop the closing of these industries and save 5,000 jobs.
Unfortunately, the Government approved what meant virtually a death warrant for the Gulf refinery in East Montreal by allowing a foreign company to purchase the refinery with the purpose of closing it. Thank God, the provincial Government, led by Mr. Robert Bourassa and Mr. Ciaccia, took over and prevented the Gulf refinery in East Montreal from closing completely! As regards the lethargy of the Conservative Government on the matter of the shipyards, I have to say quite honestly that there were certainly rather complex problems in this industry.
Unfortunately, the former Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion, the Hon. Member for Langelier (Mr. Cote), who is himself from Quebec, had plotted to ensure that the president of Versatile Vickers would be in charge of coordinating the rationalization of shipyards in Quebec. The Government told him, and this is what I found unacceptable, that if he wanted the contract for the Caribou, he had to bring together the three Quebec shipyards which I mentioned earlier, that is the two belonging to him, and one, the Sorel Shipyard, owned by the Quebec Government. Only on this condition would the Government grant him the contract for the Caribou ferry. Mr. Saunders then launched a private crusade and went to see the only other competitor, the Quebec Government, and said: "Listen, you should get into another line of work. I have a mandate from the federal Government and you should go into another field. I shall take care of the major work at the Lauzon Shipyard in Quebec City, do the little jobs in Montreal and make a lot of money, and you can do something else.
Unfortunately, I had been told about that and I must commend the Hon. Member for Richelieu (Mr. Piamondon) who also worked with the local union-and even the people, the Conservative Member had wind of the matter and he exposed that attitude. Unfortunately, the former Minister of State for Regional Industrial Expansion, the Hon. Member for Saint-Jean (Mr. Bissonnette) at that time had called me a liar, saying that it was false. But I was sure of my facts, and indeed, through the access to Information Act, I obtained the documents where it was written in black and white that the Government was committed, everything was signed, and we know what happened to the Hon. Member for Saint-Jean! When it is his word against mine-I do not think it takes very long to know who is telling the truth.

September 11, 1987
Shipbuilding
But the impact of all this is that despite this fiddling about by those politicians, or their lack of experience, the result is that today people are still talking to each other in our Quebec shipyards. Even though there are announcements of huge contracts in Quebec City, the jobs just are not there-400 employees out of 2,000 have just been recalled. In Montreal the shipyards are empty, again there are 35 employees left out of 1,500, and I know there is a problem, yes, there is a problem in the shipyard industry. Instead of having a strategy, and it is at that point that I tabled the motion, instead of this double dealing behind the workers' back, behind the union's back, when a Minister of the Crown strikes a deal with a company president and says he will give him a contract if he shuts down that one-that does not work, it will not work, the results are there. Those three scheming Ministers, where are they now? Two of them have lost their portfolios, and one has just been fired. What did that back-alley scheming produce? Nothing at all, and thank God, it shed light on the matter! This is why the proposal is that the Elouse ask the Government to strike a committee, made up of representatives from the federal Government, the Opposition in the House of Commons, the provincial Government, the Opposition in the National Assembly, the municipalities in those areas. That is important, whether it is Sorel, Quebec City, or Montreal, because those people are the area's economic future. They should be on this committee. As well as representatives from the industry, from management of course, but also from the workers.
I am confident that once such a group is set up and everyone honestly analyzes the conditions in the shipyard industry, we will discover what the problems are in Quebec, in the Atlantic region, in Ontario and in Western Canada, and what sort of work is to be done, since the contracts come under federal jurisdiction. The Mayor of Quebec City is not the one who builds boats. He may be hoodwinked by the federal Government, but he does not build boats, only the federal Government does so for the Department of National Defence or the Department of Transport, ferries and other such things.
Then the Government is aware of the new boats that are needed, of repairs which have to be done and of the orders which have to be placed. If that had been better structure than what we see now, there would not have been any crisis. Then those people would know what the capacities and the number of workers are in those shipyards. Are there too many shipyards and not enough contracts? If so, what is to be done? However, the first decision made by this Conservative Government, by the former Minister, the Member for Saint-Jean, as well as another Minister who has been sacked, the Hon. Member for Langelier (Mr. Cote) was that we had too many shipyards. They decided to close down some of them. They even schemed about which one was to be closed down and the finger was pointed at Sorel. The same thing was done in the Maritimes and in Ontario and one shipyard was expected to be closed down in the West, but the file was closed and all those changes were set aside.
Presently the shipyards in Quebec are working, but once again it is thanks to the Bourassa government, a good liberal government, thanks to Ministers like Marc-Yvan Cote, thanks to Ministers who said: Wait a minute, we cannot allow those shipyards to close down. In the Quebec City area, it was thanks to Marc-Yvan Cote that the Lauzon shipyard was kept open. It was not thanks to any Conservative Member, they did not even know where they were going. So at the provincial level they got their act together and told the federal government: Wait a minute, those shipyards have to be kept going. They created a committee and they told the federal government: We will pick up the pieces, but we do want the money. You have tampered enough with this whole matter, we want the money to have the work done.
But then again that was the provincial government which is continuously dependent on the contracts from the federal government. To top it off, the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie), after his predecessor had said there was too many shipyards, is now developing and modernizing the shipyards in his riding, in his own area. Pretty soon, this shipyard will be able to compete with the shipyards in Quebec for the maintenance of the Caribou I and Caribou II.
And governments come and go, depending on patronage, depending on the Minister, depending on the area. For all these reasons, at this moment we cannot trust anybody in this Cabinet. And I believe this is reflected in the public opinion polls.
There is nobody left with some intellectual credibility and honesty, nobody that can be trusted by the population.
In order to solve the problems shipyards are facing, there is an absolute need to set up a committee and I wish it would be a national committee. However, in this kind of matter, I believe there are regional implications, the needs are different in Quebec, in Western Canada and in the Maritimes.
But I believe it is urgent to act because in two or three years from now the same problems will arise if we do not go to the bottom of the matter.
Let us remember that during the last electoral campaign, Conservative candidates had promised to bring back full indexation of old age security pensions. You have misled the people and you promised the same thing in the shipbuilding industry.
And always the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), with one hand over his heart and the other on the Gospel: I promise you that we are going to increase the subsidies to help upgrade the shipbuilding industry. What has he done? He has done the contrary.
Well, if today the Prime Minister tells Canadiens who are listening to us: I am going to give you this. You can tell yourself right away: He has made a mistake, for he wants to take it away from us. If he says that he is going to take it away from you, it is because he is going to give it to you. Such has been the case in every matter.

Indeed, this committee could be made up of municipal and provincial representatives who, together, could find ways to ensure that the Quebec shipbuilding industry continues to exist. Our qualified labour force is an asset. The men and women who make up the labour force in this industry can compare with anybody in the world in terms of competence, quality, effectiveness and productivity. I know the Conservative Members who associate with the bosses will tell us: "They are not productive, because of three or four strikes and such and such a thing". However, that is all they care about, money. But in fact, it is not true. Just look at the figures.
Our Quebec shipyards are the most productive in all of Canada. And the quality of the job they do is superior to that of many others. We cannot give up that industry which generation after generation has been part of Quebec's heritage.
I think that one of the best ways, unless better alternatives are suggested, and I would be ready to approve them, would be to call together all parties concerned at the federal, provincial and municipal levels, labour and corporate representatives, as well as subcontractors involved as well as representatives of businessmen's groups in those areas with a specific aim, that is to keep the three Quebec shipyards in operation-and not try to close one down-but to review the orientation of those three shipyards and maintain the employment. And I am sure that with such qualified people gathered around the table, ways will be found to resolve the three above-mentioned issues that is to enable our three Quebec shipyards to maintain their orientation, to keep up employment in those shipyards at their present levels and to continue to uphold the prestige and reputation of Quebec shipyards throughout the world.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE SHIPBUILDING INDUSTRY THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A REVITALIZATION SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the issue which has been raised by the Hon. Member is an important

September 11, 1987
Shipbuilding
one and is one to which this government has recently devoted much attention. There is little doubt that this is an important industry to Canada and the severe decline in the demand for its products is not a development that can be ignored, and it will not be ignored by this government.
While the value of vessel construction work in Canadian shipbuilding and ship repairing yards averaged $191 million between 1976 and 1985 in 1971 dollars this industry suffered a 47 per cent decline from 1982 to 1984. From 1984 to 1985 the commercial order book fell by 63 per cent to a post-war low. There now remain 18 major yards in Canada following the closure or the placing in receivership of several yards in Canada: Breton Industrial Marine in Nova Scotia, the Collingwood Shipyard in Ontario, and the Bel-Aire Shipyard and two Rivtow owned yards of British Columbia. This is a direct reflection of the difficulties facing the industry.
Another indication of the problems facing this industry has been the decline in overall yard employment. While the average employment level for 1976 to 1985 stood at 15,000, by 1985 the average employment figure had declined to only 8,000. As of the end of may 1987 it totalled somewhat less than 7,000. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, it should be noted that demand is not expected to recover to the levels reached in the 1970's in the foreseeable future.
The current problems facing Canadian yards also have been felt throughout the world. The levels of orders and completions throughout the world have declined so drastically since the peak levels of the 1970's that today it is estimated there exists a 40 per cent overcapacity in shipbuilding. Specifically, while world tonnage of ships completed in 1975 was 34.2 million gross tonnes, in 1986 the tonnage completed represented about 49 per cent of that figure.
In the past year, this decline has been even more severe. For example, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) orders in Japan declined 14 per cent in the first half of 1986 in comparison to the same period in 1985. Orders declined 69 per cent in European yards over the same period. In Korea, a 77 per cent drop in the value of new shipbuilding orders was recorded over this period.
It should be noted that part of the decline in capacity utilization in some of the countries with older shipbuilding industries is due to the entrance of new aggressive competitors. Korea, China and Taiwan have all made significant additions to their shipbuilding capacities in recent years which has eroded the domination of the international market by the Western European nations and Japan.
Forecasts indicate that the world overcapacity situation will continue into the mid 1990's. As a result of the past declines in orders and the continuing difficult climate forecast for the industry, a number of countries have taken a variety of measures to address the problem.
In Japan, in the past decade there has been a 45 per cent reduction in the direct labour force involved in shipbuilding activities. Recently, a government panel called for a 20 per cent reduction in shipbuilding capacity by the end of 1987. The panel also called for mergers among builders to consolidate and rationalize the business structure of the industry and to decrease excessive competition. Two leading shipyards, Mitsui and Nippon Kokan are apparently discussing the possibility of joint capacity reductions along these lines. Kawasaki, Hitachi, and Sumitomo are talking of mergers.
In West Germany the total shipbuilding industry workforce declined from 73,000 persons in 1975 to 43,000 in 1985. It is anticipated that employment in the shipbuilding sector will fall further by roughly a quarter, or approximately 10,000 jobs. This employment is concentrated in the northern coastal areas and the German government has indicated it does not inted to attempt to maintain all of the shipbuilding capacity in these states. Instead, it looks to indutry to propose how it plans to restructure itself. To this effect the German government has announced it will provide substantial infrastructure and regional structural aid to the four northern coastal states.
In Sweden, one of the world's leading shipbuilding nations only 10 years ago, Kockums, the only remaining large new building yard, ceased new merchant vessel construction at the end of 1986.
Returning to the Canadian situation, I note the Hon. Member's request that a special committee of the house be established to consider the problems affecting the shipbuilding industry with a view to initiating a revitalization of the industry in Quebec. Such a special committee is not required since the Standing Committee on Regional Industrial Expansion is empowered, with its mandate, to study this situation. Moreover, the government is doing all that is possible to initiate a revitalization in this sector without interfering unduly in what is essentially a private sector matter. However, I welcome this opportunity to discuss the approach which the government is taking to assist the industry workers in meeting the challenge of the new environment.
There are three elements to the government strategy to deal with the situation. First, the government will continue to offer protection for the domestic market. The 25 per cent duty which applies to most vessels offers protection to Canadian shipbuilders.
Second, the government will continue to support the shipbuilding industry through its own purchases. We are fully cognizant of the important role which the government's marine requirements have had and will continue to have for this industry.
Over the past five years federal government procurements accounted for approximately 20-25 per cent of the employment in Canadian yards. The relative importance of federal procurement has been increasing steadily as commercial orders declined. As of May 26, 1987, all new building work being carried out or on order were government-related contracts.
September 11, 1987

Over the next 5 years an estimated $1.6 billion in defence procurements are expected to come on stream, accounting for approximately 38 per cent of work in Canadian shipyards. A further $700 to $1,200 million in non defence government procurements are also possible which could comprise another 25-33 per cent of total revenues in Canadian yards during the same period.
Mr. Speaker, we are working with the industry to ensure that our marine requirements are met in a fashion which acknowledges the importance of this demand to the ongoing strength of the industries while at the same time ensuring that these procurements will be provided in a manner which is cost effective to the Government.
Third, the Government has indicated that it is prepared to assist industry with a full array of its programming in adjusting itself to these new circumstances. To respond to the changed market environment and strengthen their competitive position for the future, yards will have to reduce capacity. In some cases this may require closures. In other cases, mergers, specialization, diversification or other approaches may be more appropriate. However, initiatives for responding to the new situation must come from industry.
In particular, the Government is ready to assist in industry-led restructuring plans that put Canadian yards in a better position to compete and that minimize any adverse consequences for affected workers and communities.
The first concrete instance of the application of this policy involved a restructuring proposal from the Ontario shipbuilding industry. The owners of the Collingwood shipyard came to the conclusion that they could not maintain operations in that yard. Together with owners of the other major shipyard in Ontario, they developed a plan to restructure their activities in view of the lack of demand for their products. In essence this provided that Collingwood would cease its operation and that the port Weller and port Arthur shipyards would be merged and modernized in order to be more competitive in the international market.
The Federal Government through its programs was able to assist the companies in the implementation of their plan. This was comprised of assistance under the shipbuilding industry assistance program (SIAP) for the company to move some of the more technologically advanced equipment operated in Collingwood to other facilities in Ontario. It is expected that this will result in a more competitive Ontario industry capable of servicing the needs of Great Lakes operators and better able to compete for major Crown procurements.
An area of concern to the Federal Government as well as the companies was the impact that this restructuring plan would have on the affected workers and communities. In order to minimize any possible negative effects, my colleague the Honourable Minister for Employment and Immigration selected Collingwood under the community futures program of the Canadian jobs strategy.
Shipbuilding
As you may know, the community futures program builds on the existing strengths of communities supporting the private sector and local community initiatives through a wide variety of programs. It involves a flexible cooperative effects approach and emphasizes entrepreneurial strengths.
The Government of Ontario also helped to implement the plans of the companies, by offering assistance to make the remaining yards more competitive.
The Government has also assisted owners of Quebec shipyards in reaching an agreement to consolidate ownership under Marine Industries Limited (MIL). The Government played a key role in bringing the parties together and assisted by facilitating the smooth transfer of its own contracts.
Marine Industries Limited, with its proven successful experience in the management of diversified operations, with the technological and manufacturing strengths possessed by the versatile operations and with the strong order book provided by Federal Government requirements I am sure will create a revitalized Quebec shipbuilding industry.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to re-iterate that we recognize that the shipbuilding industry is facing difficult times. The Federal Government stands ready to respond to proposals to assist the community, worker and industry to adjust to changing industry conditions. The initiatives, however must come from the private sector. The recent developments in Ontario and Quebec are clear indications of the Government's commitments in this regard.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE SHIPBUILDING INDUSTRY THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A REVITALIZATION SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on the motion of the Hon. Member for Montreal- Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart). I cannot support it fully although I agree with the Hon. Member that the shipbuilding industry is in a crisis situation.
The motion would limit the consideration of the problems affecting the shipbuilding industry and the revitalization of that industry to the Province of Quebec. While I am sure, as the Hon. Member has stated, that the shipbuilding industry in Quebec has serious problems which need to be addressed by the Government of Canada, so too does the shipbuilding industry in the rest of the country, particularly in the Atlantic provinces where there is a serious shipbuilding crisis and also on the West Coast of Canada where shipyards are closing, the workforce is growing older, and great skills associated with the shipbuilding trade are being lost.
Shipbuilding is an industry which has roots in the history of the country, from the earliest days in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and Newfoundland as a part of our great maritime industry. We are a country which borders on three oceans. We have skills associated with the industry. In the past we have had a great shipbuilding industry, but it is in a crisis. The

September 11, 1987
Shipbuilding
Government of Canada should do more than give lip service to its development.
While the previous speaker indicated that the Government does its procurement through Canadian shipyards, surely it is not enough, nor is it enough to relegate it to other existing programs.
In August, 1984, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) made a promise to the people of Canada that he would pay attention to the shipbuilding industry. In fact, at that time he said that a top priority of the PC Government would be to create a more viable and prosperous shipbuilding industry. This indicates to me that the Government of Canada made a commitment to the people of Canada back in 1984 to put into place a national shipbuilding policy.
What do we have three years later? We have an industry in crisis. Shipyards are closing in British Columbia, Nova Scotia, and Newfoundland, for example, the one at Marystown and the dockyard at St. John's, Newfoundland. They are in very serious trouble, lurching in some cases from one contract to the next and always operating very precariously without any longterm plan to guarantee jobs for skilled workers in Atlantic Canada, Quebec, and British Columbia.
We need a comprehensive policy which clearly sets out what assistance the Government will provide to the shipbuilding industry. As well we need a commitment not just to procure the shipping needs of the Government from Canadian shipyards, but to ensure the survival of the yards and the job skills for Canadians.
We have a situation, as previous speakers have indicated, where the number of people employed in the Canadian shipbuilding industry has been reduced by approximately a third over the last 10 years. We now have 7,000 or fewer people employed in that industry, whereas some 10 years of 15 years ago there were in excess of 20,000 employees. I am using the figures supplied by the General Manager of the Pictou Industries who said in a recent article that in the last 10 years 250 foreign-built vessels were registered in Canada, that is 25 a year for the last 10 years, and if those vessels had been built in Canada all Canadian shipbuilding yards would have been working to capacity. It does not seem like a great number of ships in one year, 25 for all of Canada, but if those ships had have been built in Canada instead of being registered in Canada and built in foreign countries, it would have revitalized the Canadian shipbuilding industry. We have not had the kind of commitment from this Government that would see that brought about.
The motion asks for a special committee of the House to consider the shipbuilding industry in the Province of Quebec. But there ought to be a special committee of the House not just looking at the industry in Quebec but having regard to the problems of the industry, nationally, and working toward the development promised by the Government in 1984 when it was
seeking a mandate from Canadians. In other words, the entire shipbuilding industry across the country should be looked at. With the expert advice and assistance of studies that can be undertaken by such a committee a shipbuilding policy could be put together for Canada that would guarantee its survival.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE SHIPBUILDING INDUSTRY THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A REVITALIZATION SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to take part in the debate today but first, if I may, I should like to refresh the memory of the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) about the sequence of some of the events.
As I recall, Mr. Speaker, I was with my colleague from Levis (Mr. Fontaine) the Member and Minister responsible for the Quebec region, (Mr. Cote) and all my colleagues from the greater Quebec City area when we met with the management and labour unions of Lauzon's shipyards. Mr. Speaker, I must say that, unlike my colleague from Montreal-Sainte-Marie, we were not thrown out of the yards, quite the contrary, we were warmly greated as people who were intent on helping them. Indeed 1 remember that the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie had been singled out for having been a member of the Liberal Government-it had been in office for 20 years-which had let the situation deteriorate in Canada's shipyards. They could not have cared less.
As it happens, Mr. Speaker, I am the son of a Lauzon shipyard worker. My father worked there for years, from the onset of the war and for years after that, and I have always felt a certain awareness of shipyard problems. Again recently my father was telling me that the only governments which really tried to help and solve the shipyard problems have been Conservative governments.
He reminded me that the only Government which had been willing to give contracts to the Canadian shipyards after the war was the one led by Mr. John Diefenbaker. We have to remember when the last contracts for frigates and ships were awarded by the Department National Defence. If I am not mistaken, our youngest ship was built in 1963, and the contract was awarded under the Government of Mr. John Diefenbaker. Afterwards, when the Liberals were in power, they never tried to develop a long term shipbuilding policy. As usual, they allowed the situation to deteriorate and did not try to support the modernization efforts of the shipyards or take into account the fact that most Canadian shipyards had been created because of the war effort.
These are facts which the Hon. Member for Montreal- Sainte-Marie did not mention. He tried instead to play at petty politics. Once again, he has suggested that we establish a committee. This is the latest thing among the Liberals. They create a committee when they do not want to solve a problem.
Mr. Speaker, as for creating a committee to consult, especially with members of the Opposition, I can tell you that we have better things to do! The members of the Conservative
September 11, 1987

caucus of the Quebec region, with the full support of their regional minister, have not been content to consult. We worked together and as a team to find long term solutions for the Quebec shipyards, not only for the one in Lauzon, but also for the other two major shipyards in Quebec.
It might be appropriate to note, Mr. Speaker, that between 1976 and 1985, the yearly production of the shipyards affilitated with the Canadian Shipbuilding and Ship Repairing Association averaged $191 million in constant 1971 dollars. However, this figure decreased by 47 per cent between 1982 and 1984, and the orders received by the industry went down by 63 per cent between 1984 and 1985 to reach their lowest level since the end of the Second World War.
Such is the present situation, Mr. Speaker.
Since the recent closing of five shipyards, there are now only 18 major shipyards in operation in Canada. Those which have closed recently are the Breton Industrial Marine Shipyard in Nova Scotia, the Collingwood Shipyard in Ontario, the Bel-Aire Shipyard and two Rivtow shipyards in British Columbia.
These closings, combined with the job losses incurred in all shipyards, directly reflect the problems the whole industry is facing. The average number of jobs in the industry went down from 15,000 jobs to 8,000 during the last ten years and by the end of May, 1987, there was less than 7,000 jobs left. This phenomenon is not temporary. No recovery is anticipated until the mid-1990's.
These problems are not peculiar to Canada. Naval production has suffered a significant drop in all countries, in all shipyards since the 1970's when it had reached record levels.
The worldwide industry had an overcapacity of some 40 per cent. In 1975, ships built had a total gross tonnage of some 34.2 million tonnes; the tonnage was only half as much in 1986. Last year, the drop was even more significant.
For example, according to the Organization for Economic Co-Operation and Development, OECD, orders received by shipyards in Japan among others had registered a 14 per cent drop in the first quarter of 1986 over the same period in 1985. During that period, orders received by European shipyards had dropped 69 per cent.
This worldwide drop in the orders received by shipyards reflects not only the slump the market is going through but also the changes that have occurred in the geographic distribution of the worldwide industry. The domination of the world market by Japan and Western Europe countries is challenged by the emergence of new countries, including Korea, China and Taiwan. It should be noted, however, that even Korean shipyards have suffered the repercussions of the worldwide crisis. During the last year, Korea has seen its orders drop by 77 per cent.
Shipbuilding
In the last decade, there was a 45 per cent drop in the number of direct jobs created by the shipbuilding industry in Japan. Given the circumstances, a working group set up by the Japanese Government has recommended reducing by another 20 per cent the total capacity of shipyards in Japan by the end of 1987. It has also recommended that some shipyards be merged with a view to consolidating and streamlining the industry. For instance, two major shipyards operated by the Mitsui and Nippon Kokan corporations are said to be currently discussing the possibility of jointly reducing the capacities in that order. And Kawasaki, Hitachi and Sumitomo corporations are looking at the possibilility of merging their shipyards.
In West Germany, the total manpower employed by the shipbuilding industry has declined from 73,000 in 1975 to 43,000 in 1985. And 10,000 more jobs are expected to be lost. This loss of jobs has mainly affected Northern Germany's coastal areas, and the German Government has decided it would not attempt to maintain the industry's current capacity in those areas. Instead it is relying on the industry to submit new ways of restructuring itself to that end.
Sweden's shipbuilding industry was one of the most prosperous in the world ten years ago. Kockums, the last major shipyard, stopped building new merchant ships at the end of 1986.
In Canada, the Government did all it could to revitalize the shipbuilding industry without interfering with something that is primarily a private sector matter. However, I want to take this opportunity to explain how this Government is trying to help workers.
The Government has developed a three-prong strategy to review the situation. Firstly, the Government will continue protecting the Canadian market by imposing an ad valorem duty of 25 per cent on most ships.
Secondly, the Government will pursue a supply policy encouraging the Canadian shipbuilding industry. We are fully aware of the role Government supply practices have played and will continue to play in the shipbuilding area.
For the past five years, Government purchases have allowed domestic shipyards to keep 20 to 25 per cent of their jobs. The relative significance of Government purchases has been increasing regularly as commercial orders have declined. As of May 26, 1987, all orders for new construction came either from the Government itself or from Government agencies.
Purchases estimated at $1.6 billion should be made over the next five years in the defence sector, and those contracts will account for some 38 per cent of all Canadian shipyard orders. The Government may also make additional purchases valued between $700 million and $1.2 billion. Those orders would account for an extra 25 to 33 per cent share of total domestic shipyard revenues during that period.

September 11, 1987
Shipbuilding
Thirdly, the Government has already indicated it was willing to help the shipbuilding industry better face the declining demand. Elowever, the industry will have to reduce its capacity, which may force it to close down some yards or take alternative steps such as mergers, specializing or diversifying. The initiative however must come from the industry.
The Government is willing to help the industry implement restructuring programs capable of helping shipyards better compete, thereby reducing the negative impact on workers and communities.
The restructuring program developed by the Ontario shipbuilding industry was the first concrete result of that offer. The owners of the Collingwood shipyard have come to the conclusion that they could no longer operate the shipyard. With the owners of another major Ontario shipyard, they developed a program to reorganize their operations, essentially by closing the Collingwood shipyard and merging and modernizing the Port Weller and Port Arthur shipyards to make them more competitive.
Mr. Speaker, I could go on for quite some time speaking about various matters related to the shipyards, but we have to remember that, especially in the case of the Quebec shipyards, when the Lauzon workers had major problems last winter and were expecting some assistance, the federal Government did not hesitate to try to help them through various training and retraining programs, and so on, especially in the great region of Quebec. In this regard, Mr. Speaker, I would like to underline the hard work of my colleague for Levis (Mr. Fontaine), who right from the start, has taken an interest in the shipyards and worked vigorously with the full support of all his colleagues from the Quebec Conservative caucus to find rational, logical and effective solutions to the real problems of shipbuilding in Canada, and it is not by creating so-called committees, such as suggested by the well-known Liberal prophet of doom and gloom, the Hon. Member for Montreal- Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart), that we can find real answers to the problems affecting the shipbuilding industry in Canada.

although we have heard a number of remarks aimed at undermining the suggestion advocated by the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart), I should like to indicate that what concerns me most after listening to Hon. Members who rose after my colleague from Montreal- Sainte-Marie is the fact that the Government has no intention of responding to the legitimate request that a committee be established to make an exhaustive study of measures required to keep Quebec's shipyards in operation. The only thing we are asking the Government to do is to strike a committee which would provide these workers and these regions which have been hard hit-shutdowns, fewer
contracts, series of measures taken by governments or management-which would provide these people with an opportunity to sit at a table and attempt to find solutions to the problems which have plagued these regions which I call designated. Sadly enough, the fact that the Government is not interested in entertaining this request will probably lead to a situation such that things will simply grow worse, and the first thing we will know is that there will be yet more lay-offs in the various regions involved, be it in Quebec City, Montreal or Sorel.
I think that if the government had agreed or would agree to consider this proposal seriously, it would provide representatives of both the government and the official Opposition with an opportunity to sit down not only to complain about what was not done or could have been done, but also to get together with representatives of the municipal and provincial governments. I suggest that if the government had agreed or would agree to this proposal, the workers of these shipyards would be delighted to say that the federal government is assuming at last its responsibilities and taking some action to help preserve and protect their jobs.
The situation is about the same in other industries, so that when representatives from various groups . . . The situation is almost identical in the case of the pollution of the Saint-Maurice River where groups should meet and for which the department or government should create a sort of committee on which they could sit. Unfortunately, we are aware that the Government is unwilling to give individuals faced with a problem a chance to discuss it, to sit around a table and find solutions to problems about which there is no co-operation and when I say co-operation, I mean at the local, regional, municipal, provincial and federal levels. Mr. Speaker, obviously this government recognizes the tragic situation facing the shipbuilding industry, but the same solution is always offered, namely that we should establish a committee to address the problem.
With opposite members, the choice is either to establish a committee or to build ships. We heard the same old thing a moment ago from a guy who long on empty and ludicrous rhetoric blamed everybody around to finally come up with a nice solution of his own.
September 11, 1987

Mr. Speaker, I think that in spite of all the wonderful solutions we might have, we should still take into consideration the world situation. At the present time there is an overcapacity in shipbuilding, when supply exceeds demand, and in fact, on the international market, we build more ships than we need.
That does not mean we should stop shipbuilding altogether. But 1 fail to see how a committee could solve that problem. It might put forward some answers.
I listened to my colleagues from the New Democratic Party and the Liberal Party when they said that the good Liberal provincial government had decided to act on its own. But let them go ahead and build ships for they too have a shipbuilding industry. The federal government operates Coast Guard vessels and icebreakers and also ferries. Let them build many ferries and we will then have a better service between Matane and Riviere-du-Loup, every half hour for instance. These obviously are not practical solutions but that's the story.
It is not the government responsibility to make up for the international market's deficiencies. But if there is now an overproduction of ships, if other countries build them at lower
Shipbuilding
costs, will a policy oblige Canadian shipowners, if there are any, to buy strictly Canadian products? That does not work either. Should we build ships just for the sake of keeping shipyards in operation? It is not workable either.
So we must pick more realistic options. The only one is to establish an economic climate which will bring about an improvement of the situation.
Mr. Speaker, more jobs have been created over the past three years than in the previous decade and a half. Interest rates, the inflation level are some of the factors which will allow those people to survive or retrain.
